Hi Samira — thanks for the clear questions. Quick answers up front, then examples below.

Short answers:
- We bill for what is sent to and returned from the model: system + user + tool outputs that are embedded into the model request/response. Tool outputs that are relayed into the model response are billed as output tokens.
- Rounding is applied per API request: we count tokens at token-granularity (no fractional tokens), and each request's input and output totals are rounded up to the next whole token where applicable, then summed for that request.
- There is no automatic per-customer free prefix cache on the hosted API that zeros billed input — billed tokens equal what is actually sent. That said, our Optimize tooling can suggest prefix resizing or static prompt strategies to reduce per-request input size.

Detailed examples (to illustrate):
Example A — simple chat turn:
- system prompt: 120 tokens
- user message: 80 tokens
- model generates: 200 tokens
Billed = 120 + 80 + 200 = 400 tokens for that request (each component tokenized and added).

Example B — function/tool call which returns content that the model then includes in the response:
- system prompt: 50 tokens
- user message: 40 tokens
- tool (search) returns payload: 405 tokens
- model response that includes and expands on tool content: 150 tokens
Billed = 50 + 40 + 405 + 150 = 645 tokens. The tool payload is treated as output-side content for billing because it is returned to the model/response path.

Streaming notes:
- Tokens generated while streaming are counted as output tokens (same as non-streamed output). Rounding happens at the request level — we don’t round each streaming chunk separately. If a streaming response produces e.g. 154.2 token-equivalents during generation, the final generated token count will be rounded up to 155 for that request.

Edge cases:
- If you do an initial request that primes a long context and then subsequent requests use the same context via client-side reuse (i.e., you don’t resend the long system prompt), only the tokens you actually send are billed. Redwood doesn’t automatically eliminate billed tokens just because prompts match across requests — billed tokens are based strictly on request payloads.

Adding a couple of engineering clarifications on subtle cases we've seen in other large POCs: 

• Function / JSON arguments: when a model emits structured arguments (JSON) that contain long keys/URLs, those are tokenized and billed on the output side. If you then send the argument payload back in a follow-up request as "user content" you're billed again for that input. Consider passing only IDs in repeated round trips to avoid double-billing.

• Streaming + tool stitching: when multiple micro-tool calls are stitched into a single streamed response (e.g., search results merged into narrative), our billing counts the full tokenized tool payload once per request. Watch for repeated append patterns that resend the same large tool payload.

• Rounding behavior: because we round at the request level, a pattern of many tiny requests (e.g., 2–3 token prompts) can cost relatively more due to per-request rounding overhead. For heavy throughput POCs, batching small items into a single request often reduces billed tokens.

If ACME wants an engineering walkthrough, we can run a short tokenization audit on a sample of your messages (we'll produce a CSV showing token-by-component). It helps finance and SREs validate estimates.

—Karthik
